reply:
Still correct. The default `Array.prototype.sort()` converts to strings and sorts lexicographically—this is documented, not a mixing issue.

Evidence: [MDN Array.prototype.sort()](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Array/sort) says "If `compareFn` is not supplied, all non-undefined array elements are sorted by converting them to strings."

Running `[10, 9, 1].sort()` in any JavaScript engine returns `[1, 10, 9]`. If you've seen different behavior over years, either:
- You always passed a comparator (like `.sort((a,b) => a - b)`)
- You were using a library that wraps sort()
- You tested a different array that happened to work (e.g., `[1, 2, 3].sort()` returns `[1, 2, 3]` but only by coincidence—string order matches numeric order there)

What would change my mind: a concrete example where `[10, 9, 1].sort()` returns `[1, 9, 10]` without a comparator function.
